title: A daily slope larger than maxAmount turns the rate limit into a burst cap rather than a cumulative exposure cap
content:
Spark's rate limits are defined by exactly two parameters, described in each instance's `Rate Limits` document (e.g. A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.1.2.2.4): "The current `maxAmount` and `slope` for this conduit's inflow/outflow". `maxAmount` is the ceiling on available capacity; `slope` is the rate at which that capacity regenerates per day — a leaky-bucket / recharging-allowance design rather than a fixed period quota.

The non-obvious consequence appears when the two numbers are compared. USDC inflow: `maxAmount` 100,000,000 against `slope` 200,000,000 per day. USDT inflow: `maxAmount` 500,000,000 against `slope` 2,000,000,000 per day. wETH inflow: `maxAmount` 50,000 ETH against `slope` 250,000 ETH per day. In each case the slope refills the entire bucket several times over in a single day — twelve minutes to two hours of regeneration to restore a fully drained USDT allowance.

So `maxAmount` is not a cap on total exposure that can be built; it is a cap on how much can be moved *at one moment*. Sustained deployment is bounded by `slope`, and where slope is set multiples above maxAmount, sustained deployment is effectively unbounded relative to the headline ceiling.

That is a defensible design if the intent is to bound blast radius per transaction and force large reallocations to be visible as a sequence of actions over time. It is a misreading of the parameters if a reader treats `maxAmount` as the risk limit for the venue. The Dai instance is the exception that proves the point: `maxAmount` 100,000,000 with `slope` 50,000,000 per day means a full drain genuinely takes two days to restore.
description: Capacity regenerates linearly at slope per day up to a maxAmount ceiling; where slope exceeds maxAmount the bucket refills within hours, so only single-transaction size is truly constrained.
